newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS-Las Cristinas mine bogged down in legal war.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Las Cristinas mine bogged down in legal war.

text.p: An end to the bitter legal battle between Placer Dome and Crystallex for Venezuela's gold rich Las Cristinas concession is far from over, lawyers said.

And while both sides acknowledged that Crystallex has now gained access to the Supreme Court, the company still faces many hurdles on the long road to victory, not least the government's stake in the success of its partnership with Placer in potentially the largest gold mine in South America.

The most recent exchange of legal fire re-opened Tuesday when an admissions chamber barred three out of eleven motions of Crystallex's claim for the lucrative Las Cristinas 4 and 6 concessions from entering the Supreme Court -- because the statute of limitations had expired.

Investors, spooked by the Byzantine procedures of Venezuela's legal system, dumped Crystallex shares. Yet, the chamber also allowed entry to several other motions and, "under Venezuelan law you cannot be a little bit pregnant," Crystallex lawyer Ricardo Cottin told Reuters Friday.
"We're exactly where we want to be ... We always wanted our case to be examined by the Supreme Court. That's always been our strategy, and that's what we have achieved," he added.
Crystallex shares lost some 50 percent on Wednesday, closing at C$3.80 but had moved ahead to C$4.55 Friday as the company embarked on an information campaign.

"The admitted motions will be reviewed and decided by the five Justices (of the Supreme Court's Political Administrative Chamber) as part of its regular procedure, and the remaining three motions will be reviewed and decided by the five Justices at the same time through a guaranteed process of appeal," Crystallex said in a press release.
The end legal result is "the same as if every motion were admitted by the July 15 action," the release added.

However, lawyers at rival company Placer Dome, which has a 70/30 joint venture with state holding company Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana (CVG) to develop the $576 million project, said pre-construction at the site would start shortly, despite Crystallex's cries of victory.
"Most probably we're going to go ahead with construction of the camp ... both CVG and ourselves feel that secure," said Jose Antonio Pinedo, legal counsel for the project.

Lawyers for both companies said subsequent proceedings could carry on for years. With judges due to take their summer holidays shortly, Pineda said consideration of Crystallex's appeal alone "could take some four to five months."
"If they loose the appeal, their battle is over for the gold," Pineda added. "But if they win (the appeal), there's still a final Supreme Court decision pending."

Pineda said Placer's case would focus on a number of alleged irregularities in the long and often convoluted chain of ownership between the mine's original concessionaire -- the elderly Dot Culvert Whitney Lemon who died heirless and alone in 1986 -- and Crystallex.
Any final Crystallex victory may also prove pyrrhic in the face of a government that has touted its association with Placer as an emblem of a much-vaunted mining opening.

Former Crystallex business associate Jack Kaplan, who worked with the company on the financing of Crystallex's Albino concession which abuts the Cristinas site, told Reuters: "even if they win the case, there's some very major things they have to get including environmental permits, and it's not clear the government would be so willing."
Crystallex executives have repeatedly said they are willing to negotiate a settlement with Placer. But Placer spokesman Felipe Ruiz told Reuters: "Never. It's a matter of principal."
